notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024, as the county reported them to the Census Bureau's Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
The county borrowed $50,917,000 during the year, which is not counted as revenue but helps explain spending above revenue.
Debt service leaves out $8,756,000 of principal repaid with new borrowing the county did not spend on capital that year, most likely refinancing or a rolled-over note.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.
Political money is not scored: contributions to New Mexico county candidates were not loaded.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-20. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals, corporate tax breaks and license-plate cameras mapped by volunteers have not been checked for New Mexico yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024, as the city reported them to the Census Bureau's Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included. Residents also pay Sandoval County.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
The city borrowed $424,000 during the year, which is not counted as revenue but helps explain spending above revenue.
Payments to other governments ($317,000) are left out, because the government receiving them reports that spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.
Political money is not scored: contributions to New Mexico city candidates were not loaded.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Cameras: 25 license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Rio Rancho's borders in OpenStreetMap (23 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-20. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for New Mexico yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: Flock camera network
redFlags.detail: 23 Flock Safety license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Rio Rancho's borders in OpenStreetMap. Flock cameras photograph every passing car and feed a search network shared with police agencies across the country. Who runs each camera is not recorded; cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies are not counted.

source.label: OpenStreetMap license-plate cameras (as mapped by DeFlock)

redFlags.label: Face recognition
redFlags.detail: The Rio Rancho Police Department began a three-year trial of Clearview AI face recognition software in 2023.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS013577, citing KOB

redFlags.label: Gunshot detection (ShotSpotter)
redFlags.detail: Rio Rancho Public Schools indicated that it was seeking $1.5 million from the state for gunshot detection in the district's 10 elementaries and four middle schools and that it had funds to install the system in two high schools. The district reported that the project for the two high schools was completed in 2019.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS009158, citing Albuquerque Journal

redFlags.label: License-plate readers
redFlags.detail: The Rio Rancho Police Department obtained automated license plate readers in 2018.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS007459, citing KOAT

redFlags.label: Private camera registry
redFlags.detail: The Rio Rancho Police Department started a registry of surveillance cameras voluntarily submitted by local residents and businesses in 2015.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS002564, citing KRQE

redFlags.label: Police drones
redFlags.detail: The Rio Rancho Police Department operates one DJI Inspire drone as of 2018, according to data compiled by the Center for the Study of the Drone at Bard College.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS003780, citing Center for the Study of the Drone at Bard College
